A RAG pipeline consists of two halves that run at different times: indexing and query time [1]. Indexing happens ahead of time, whenever documents are added or changed [1]. Query time happens for every question [1].

During indexing, documents are split into passages, often between 200 and 500 tokens, and then embedded into a vector index [1]. The vector index allows for quick searching of the passages [1]. Indexing can be slow, but it runs in the background and can take an hour to index a collection of 50,000 pages [1].

On query time, the system embeds the question and searches for relevant passages using a vector index and/or keyword search [5]. The top candidates are retrieved, and then a reranker is used to rank the candidates [5]. The reranker keeps the top 3 to 8 candidates [5]. A prompt is then built using the instructions, question, and passages [5]. The model generates an answer using the prompt [5].

RAG pipelines can be prone to errors, particularly in retrieval and reranking [2]. Retrieval misses can occur when the retriever does not bring back the correct passages, and ranking problems can happen when the right chunk is retrieved but lands below several plausible but unhelpful chunks [2]. Conflicting sources can also occur when old and new versions of a policy both live in the index [2].

To improve the performance of a RAG pipeline, teams can measure retrieval and answers separately, and add complexity such as reranking or hybrid search only when the numbers tell them that they need it [5]. The quality of the documents also matters, and teams should take the time to clean and prepare the documents before implementing a RAG pipeline [8].

In a worked example, a user asks a question, and the RAG pipeline finds relevant passages using a hybrid search and reranking [8]. The pipeline then builds a prompt using the instructions, question, and passages, and the model generates an answer [8]. The final answer is confirmed to be accurate by checking the citations [8].

Overall, RAG pipelines are a useful tool for making AI more accurate and reliable, particularly when used in conjunction with proper indexing, retrieval, and generation [5]. By understanding how RAG pipelines work and how to improve their performance, teams can create more effective and efficient AI systems [5].

A RAG pipeline works by combining two main components: retrieval and generation [1]. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a technique used to improve the accuracy and reliability of language models by retrieving relevant documents and using them to generate answers [1]. The pipeline consists of two phases: an offline phase that prepares the documents, and an online phase that runs for each question [6].

During the offline phase, the documents are prepared by splitting them into passages, embedding the passages, and indexing the embeddings [6]. The passages are typically around 200 to 800 tokens in length, with an overlap of 10 to 20 percent to ensure that sentences at the edges are not lost [6]. The embeddings are then stored in a vector index, and optionally, a keyword index is built over the same chunks [6].

In the online phase, the question is embedded using the same embedding model as the documents [6]. The embedded question is then searched against the vector index to retrieve the nearest chunks [6]. The retrieved chunks are then merged and reranked, keeping the top 3 to 10 [6]. The reranked candidates are then used to build a prompt, which includes an instruction to answer only from the passages and to cite them [6]. The model is then asked to generate an answer based on the prompt [6].

The quality of the RAG pipeline can be improved by adjusting various parameters, such as the chunk size, overlap, and the number of candidates retrieved [6]. The pipeline can also be improved by adding additional steps, such as a reranker or a second model to check the answer against the retrieved text [5]. Logging the retrieved chunks for every question can also help identify where the pipeline is failing [5].

Despite its potential, the RAG pipeline is not without its limitations. It can be prone to retrieval misses, ranking problems, conflicting sources, and answering anyway [5]. These issues can be addressed by adjusting the pipeline's parameters, adding additional steps, and logging the retrieved chunks [5].

Evaluating a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system is crucial to ensure its accuracy and effectiveness. A golden test set, comprising a fixed list of questions with known good answers, is the foundation of RAG evaluation [1]. The size of the test set depends on the size of the change to be detected, with larger sets providing more accurate results [1]. Paired comparisons, where two versions of a system are compared on the same questions, are more sensitive than overall rate comparisons [1].

In addition to retrieval metrics, such as recall@k and precision@k, answer metrics, including faithfulness, answer correctness, and citation accuracy, are also essential [2]. Human review is the most reliable but slow, while using a model judge calibrated against human grades can provide faster and more accurate results [2]. The test set should include real user questions, questions across all major topics and document types, and hard cases such as ambiguous questions and questions with no answer in the corpus [2].

A minimal evaluation routine involves running the test set on every change to chunking, retrieval, or prompts, and tracking the results over time [3]. This routine takes an hour or two for a test set of 100 questions and costs little compared to a bad release [3]. To ensure the system is working, teams should track recall@5, faithfulness, answer correctness, and format failure rate on 100 to 200 real questions [5].

Online evaluation is also crucial, as it watches live traffic and provides explicit feedback, implicit signals, and logs enough data to diagnose each failure [7]. Sample answers for review every week can catch problems that metrics miss, such as subtle misreadings and outdated documents [7]. Finally, feeding what is learned back into the offline test set keeps the test set close to what users actually ask [7].

In conclusion, evaluating a RAG system requires a combination of offline tests, online monitoring, and continuous feedback from users. By following a minimal evaluation routine and using a variety of metrics, teams can ensure their RAG system is accurate, effective, and reliable.
